article.overview: A sample sorting system separates collected material into defined groups, most commonly by particle size, before the material is delivered to an analysis instrument, a storage container or a return capsule. On a planetary surface it would normally sit between a collection device (scoop, drill or core tool) and the instruments or containers that need small, well-defined portions. No flight-proven sample sorting system for lunar surface operations was identified in the sources consulted for this article. The best-documented flight example is the sieving and portioning hardware on NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars, while the most relevant lunar precedents are the sieving practices used in Apollo sample curation and the Chang'e 5 surface sampling and packing system, which collected and sealed samples but did not sort them.
article.description: A sample sorting system receives material from a collection device and divides it. The most common sorting basis is particle size. Material is passed through one or more sieves, and the fraction that passes each sieve is kept, rejected or routed onward. Fine material may be sent to an analytical instrument, coarse material may be returned to the collector, and the division may also be used to create replicate portions for different instruments or containers. The concept is simple, but the engineering is not. The following engineering considerations are general and are not drawn from a specific verified source: lunar regolith is abrasive and electrostatically active, sticky samples can bridge or clog sieve openings, and any sorting step adds surfaces that must be cleaned or protected from cross-contamination. A sorting system therefore has to deal with mechanical transport (commonly by vibration, gravity or tilting), containment, sample traceability and the risk of changing the material it is meant to characterise. The term 'sorting' is used here in its broad sense. In the sources consulted, the sorting functions are usually called sieving, sizing, portioning or sample processing. The article uses the catalogue name exactly as given and treats these functions as the relevant class of hardware.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Sorting by size improves the quality of many downstream measurements. Instruments that analyse powdered material often need particles below a set size so that the sample is representative, can be introduced through a small inlet and does not block the instrument. Size-separated fractions also allow scientists to compare material of different grain sizes, which is the kind of comparison a single unsorted sample cannot provide. Curation of returned samples has a similar purpose. For the Apollo 17 remaining sample, the material was sieved into size fractions and each fraction was weighed (Gross et al., 2024). A sorting system that operates on the Moon could extend this approach by performing the separation in situ, before samples are sealed for return or delivered to a local analyser. Applications proposed or implied by the sources include: preparation of powdered samples for analytical instruments with inlet size limits; separation of fine material for measurements that depend on grain size; splitting of a sample into portions for different instruments or containers; rejection of oversized material so that it does not enter an instrument or container; and preparation of samples for lunar resource characterisation, although no lunar resource-processing system was verified in this review.
article.operating_principle: The simplest operating principle is gravity-assisted sieving. A sample is placed on or fed into a screen with defined openings. Particles smaller than the opening pass through and are collected below. Particles larger than the opening remain on the screen and are either returned, discarded or passed to a second screen. Multi-stage sieves allow more than one size class to be separated in one operation. Vibration is commonly used to help material move and pass through openings. NASA Tech Brief NPO-46334 describes a compact, low-mass mechanism that uses low-frequency vibration to transport powdered cuttings and soil grains from a sampling device and to sort them by particle size, with the stated intention of use on landers or rovers (Sherrit et al., 2010). The tech brief describes the need and the function; the consulted record does not describe the vibration mechanism in detail. The Curiosity rover's CHIMRA device provides a flown example of a sieving approach. NASA's Photojournal captions state that material from the rover's scoop or drill is passed through a 150-micrometre sieve before portions are delivered to instruments (NASA Photojournal, PIA16691). The consulted abstracts do not describe the detailed sorting mechanics, so no further mechanism is attributed to them here.
article.scientific_importance: The scientific importance of a sample sorting system lies less in the act of sorting itself than in what it makes possible. Representative, size-controlled samples improve the reliability of instrument measurements, and separated fractions allow comparisons that unsorted material cannot support. Apollo sample curation produced size-resolved records of lunar soil for the samples it processed (Gross et al., 2024). Mars sample handling on Curiosity demonstrated that a rover can sieve and portion powdered rock and soil and deliver portions to onboard analytical instruments (Jandura, 2010; NASA Photojournal). For a future lunar mission, sorting in situ could reduce the amount of unsorted material that must be returned or transported, and it could allow an instrument to receive a predictable sample. The importance of this capability depends on the specific science objectives and cannot be assessed generically.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a sample sorting system. Sorting hardware ranges from a manual sieve stack in a curation laboratory to a rover-mounted processing device with actuators, sieves, chambers and portioning mechanisms. Mass, dimensions and power are therefore tied to the named example and its source. Where a value was not published in the consulted sources, it is reported as not publicly specified.

examples.name: Apollo lunar sample curation sieving (ground laboratory practice)
examples.type: Historical ground curation practice; not a flight payload
examples.description: Apollo lunar soils were separated into size fractions during curation. For the Apollo 17 remaining-sample procedure, NASA describes sieving the remaining sample into fractions of less than 1 mm, 1-2 mm, 2-4 mm and 4-10 mm, with each fraction weighed (Gross et al., 2024). This was laboratory processing on Earth rather than a flown payload, and no hardware mass, dimensions or power for the sieving equipment were found in the consulted sources.
examples.sorting_basis: Particle size (sieving), followed by weighing of each fraction
examples.qualification: Not spaceflight hardware. No equipment mass, dimensions or power were found in the consulted source.

examples.name: Curiosity Collection and Handling for In-situ Martian Rock Analysis (CHIMRA)
examples.type: Flown Mars sample-handling device (not a lunar payload)
examples.description: CHIMRA is a sample acquisition and processing device on NASA's Mars Science Laboratory rover Curiosity. It receives powdered material from the rover's scoop or drill and sieves it through a 150-micrometre screen, then delivers portions to onboard instruments through a portion box (NASA Photojournal, PIA16691; Jandura, 2010). The Jandura abstract states that the system 'sorts the samples into fine particles through sieving' and delivers small portions to two instruments inside the rover. NASA/JPL later described a second scoop of dune sand that was processed through a coarser 1 mm sieve in addition to the 150-micrometre screen (NASA JPL, January 2016). CHIMRA has been operated on Mars, as shown by the 2012-2013 photographs and captions, but the consulted sources do not provide verified mass, dimensions or power values for the device, so these fields are reported as not publicly specified.
examples.outputs: Portions delivered to onboard analytical instruments (SAM and CheMin) through a portion box (NASA Photojournal, PIA16691 and PIA16766)
examples.qualification: Operated on Mars according to NASA Photojournal captions. Mass, dimensions and power were not verified in the consulted sources.

examples.name: Chang'e 5 Surface Sampling and Packing System
examples.type: Flown lunar sample-collection and packaging system (not a sorting system)
examples.description: The Chang'e 5 mission carried a Surface Sampling and Packing System developed by a Hong Kong Polytechnic University team with the China Academy of Space Technology. The system collected lunar regolith with two samplers, sealed the sample container and transferred it into the ascender. The release describes Sampler A (about 35 cm, shovel-shaped for loose regolith) and Sampler B (about 30 cm, toothed flaps and an internal piston for sticky material), each with a near-field camera rated to 130 C. The sealing and packaging unit has a stated mass of 1.5 kg and the sample container a stated mass of 360 g. The release gives no overall system mass. The system performed collection and packaging on the Moon after the probe landed on 1 December 2020 but did not sort material by size. The release is an institutional account and has not been checked against an independent engineering document.
examples.qualification: Flown on Chang'e 5 according to the PolyU release. The release is institutional and not independently checked. No overall system mass was stated.

examples.name: Low-frequency vibration particle transport and size-sorting mechanism (NASA Tech Brief NPO-46334)
examples.type: Proposed or prototype concept (flight status not stated in the consulted record)
examples.description: NASA Tech Brief NPO-46334 describes a mechanism that transports and sieves powdered cuttings and soil grains by particle size using low-frequency vibration. The stated application is compact, low-mass sample handling for landers or rovers, and the mechanism is intended to move sorted particles to analytical instruments (Sherrit et al., 2010). The consulted NTRS record does not state whether the mechanism has been built, tested in a relevant environment or flown. It is therefore treated as a proposed concept or prototype. No mass, dimensions, power, sieve openings or vibration frequencies were verified.
examples.function: Transport and size-sort powdered cuttings and soil grains; intended for lander or rover use
examples.qualification: Concept or prototype status not stated in the consulted NTRS record. Full text not reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions can be applied to a generic lunar sample sorting system. The dimensions of the examples above are either not publicly specified in the consulted sources or belong to different systems. The Chang'e 5 sampler lengths (about 35 cm and about 30 cm) belong to a collection system, not a sorter. The CHIMRA dimensions and the Apollo sieving equipment dimensions were not verified. Any future sorter's dimensions would need to be set by its sieve and portion requirements, its mounting arrangement and its containment environment.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only verified mass figures in this article are the Chang'e 5 sealing and packaging unit (1.5 kg) and sample container (360 g), which belong to a collection and packaging system rather than a sorter. No mass is publicly specified in the consulted sources for CHIMRA, the Apollo sieving equipment or the NPO-46334 mechanism. Mass should not be inferred from the examples above.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power requirement was verified for any sample sorting system in the consulted sources. The Chang'e 5 release does not give a power figure for the packaging system. The power requirement of a future sorter would depend on its actuation method, for example vibration or motorised tilting, and would need to be defined from the verified design of that system.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar sample sorting system would operate in vacuum, across large surface temperature variations and under abrasive dust exposure. The Chang'e 5 release describes the sun-facing lunar surface reaching about 110 C and the system being exposed to vacuum, solar wind and cosmic rays (PolyU, 2020). These conditions also affect sorting hardware: lubricants and seals must survive, sieves must resist abrasion, and electronics and actuators must tolerate thermal cycling. Sorting introduces additional operational requirements. Sieve openings can be blocked by fine or sticky material, so the system needs a way to clear or replace screens. Mechanical vibration can disturb nearby instruments, which is why the CHIMRA design isolates the intentional vibration environment from sensitive instruments (Jandura, 2010). NASA's Curiosity sample-processing experience included a first decontamination exercise on the CHIMRA tool (NASA Photojournal, PIA16194), which indicates that sample-processing hardware needs cleaning before it handles new material. Containment is another requirement, particularly for sample-return missions. Sorting should take place inside a controlled environment, and any loss of sealed containment would compromise the sample. These requirements are general engineering considerations and are not specific to a verified lunar design.
article.limitations: The main limitation is the absence of a flight-proven lunar sample sorting system in the consulted sources. The Curiosity CHIMRA device sorts on Mars, the Chang'e 5 system collected and packaged samples on the Moon without sorting, and the Apollo sieving was performed in curation laboratories. Each example addresses part of the function, but none demonstrates a lunar surface sorting payload. Sieving also has limits. Particles coarser than the sieve openings are rejected by design, and fine material may stick to surfaces or screens. As a general engineering consideration, a sorting step can change the size distribution of the material it handles, so its effect must be understood before results are interpreted. This article has not verified a measured size-distribution bias for any specific sorting device.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A sample sorting system could be delivered to the Moon as part of a surface payload, a sample-processing package or a rover-mounted instrument. No lunar lander, rover or sample-return architecture has been verified as carrying such a system, so no compatibility claim is made in this article.
transportation_process: Surface payload: integrate the system on Earth with its power, thermal and data interfaces.
Surface payload: launch it and transfer it towards the Moon.
Surface payload: deliver it to the surface with a lunar lander.
Surface payload: deploy or position it, level it if required and connect power and communications.
Surface payload: connect the inlet to a collection device (robotic arm or astronaut-operated tool) and define the outputs as instrument inlets or sealed containers.
Rover or mobile payload: stow the system during transit, mount it where it can receive samples from the collection tool and deliver sorted material to instruments or containers.
Sample-return payload: sort inside a containment environment, seal the portions and transfer them into the return chain with contamination control, sealing verification and traceability at each step.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For a stand-alone surface payload, deployment would follow lander delivery, positioning and interface connection. For a rover-mounted system, deployment would be the mounting and operation on the rover's sample-handling arm or turret. The Curiosity CHIMRA example shows a rover-mounted architecture on Mars: the device sits on the rover's turret, takes material from the scoop or drill and delivers portions to instruments (NASA Photojournal, PIA16691). Its operating interfaces are part of a much larger rover system, and they cannot be transferred to a lunar rover without a verified interface definition.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Curiosity's CHIMRA is a flown rover-mounted example of in situ sieving and portioning on Mars (NASA Photojournal, PIA16691; Jandura, 2010). Chang'e 5 is a flown lunar example of surface collection and packaging of samples for return, although it did not sort material by size (PolyU, 2020). Apollo curation sieving is a ground-laboratory example and was not a flown payload (Gross et al., 2024).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: A future sample sorting system's compatibility with a particular lunar lander, rover or return vehicle would need to be assessed using its mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power and data interfaces, sample-transfer method and containment requirements. No lander, rover or sample-return architecture has been verified as compatible with a sorting system, so no compatibility claim is made. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by user instruction and are not included.

article.historical_significance: Sample sorting by size has a long history in planetary science. Apollo sample curation separated lunar soils into fractions and weighed them, producing size-resolved records for the samples it processed (Gross et al., 2024). The Apollo 17 procedure is an example of ground-based sorting of lunar material by size. Curiosity's CHIMRA is a significant flown example of in situ sieving on another planet. NASA's Photojournal captions describe the first sample of its kind acquired from the interior of a Martian rock being delivered to instruments through the CHIMRA system (NASA Photojournal, PIA16766). Chang'e 5 demonstrated that a robotic lunar surface system could collect and seal samples for return to Earth after the mission landed on 1 December 2020 (PolyU, 2020). These achievements provide practical experience with sample handling but do not establish a lunar sorting payload.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flight-proven lunar sample sorting system was identified. Claims about lunar sorting hardware are limited to proposals, ground practice and adjacent flown systems. The Sherrit et al. (2010) tech brief is an NTRS catalogue record and abstract; its full text was not reviewed, and its flight, prototype and test status is not stated in the consulted record. The Sunshine (2010) and Jandura (2010) papers were reviewed through NTRS abstracts only, and their full texts may contain specifications that were not verified here. CHIMRA mass, dimensions, power and sieve tolerances were not verified; the 150-micrometre sieve opening and portion-box delivery are supported by NASA Photojournal captions and the Jandura abstract. The Chang'e 5 dimensions and masses come from a PolyU institutional release and have not been checked against an independent engineering document. The Apollo 17 sieving fractions are taken from a 2024 NASA conference paper; equipment specifications and the environment of the Lunar Receiving Laboratory were not verified. Several search results were not used because their content could not be verified: an ESA Sample Transfer Arm report, a student lunar regolith sorting concept, and a 2026 university poster on legged-robot sample sorting. A Society of Automotive Engineers article on the vibration mechanism could not be retrieved for review. No direct verified image was identified for the Chang'e 5 system or the Apollo sieving practice. No lunar landing site, lander compatibility or mission-specific deployment is assumed.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: No flight-proven lunar sample sorting system was identified. The payload class is documented here through ground curation practice, a flown Mars sample-processing device, a flown lunar collection and packaging system that does not sort, and a proposed or prototype vibration size-sorting mechanism.
CHIMRA mass, dimensions, power and sieve tolerances were not verified. Mass, dimensions and power are reported as null, not as estimates.
The Sherrit et al. (2010) tech brief was reviewed through its NTRS catalogue record only. Flight, prototype and test status are not stated in the consulted record.
The Sunshine (2010) and Jandura (2010) papers were reviewed through NTRS abstracts only. Full texts were not reviewed.
The Chang'e 5 dimensions and masses come from a PolyU institutional press release, which has not been checked against an independent engineering document. The release gives no overall system mass.
The Apollo 17 sieving fractions come from a 2024 NASA conference paper (Gross et al.). Apollo sieving equipment specifications and Lunar Receiving Laboratory environment details were not verified.

The 1 mm coarser sieve is taken from a NASA JPL news article dated 21 January 2016 that describes a dune sand sampling sequence on Curiosity. The article does not name CHIMRA explicitly in the parts reviewed; the attribution to CHIMRA is inferred from the sieve hardware described.

Search results that could not be verified and were not used: an ESA Sample Transfer Arm report, a student lunar regolith sorting concept, a 2026 university poster on legged-robot sample sorting (text unreadable), and a Society of Automotive Engineers article on the vibration mechanism (retrieval refused by the fetch tool).

Image verification: the three NASA Photojournal direct JPEG assets were checked for HTTP 200 and image/jpeg content type, and their source pages were fetched. Full-resolution downloads were not checked. Reuse conditions are set by NASA media guidelines and were not reviewed in full; public-domain status is not assumed.
No direct verified image was identified for the Chang'e 5 system or the Apollo sieving practice, so no image entries are provided for those examples.
Captions for NASA Photojournal images are paraphrased from the source pages rather than quoted in full.
